passage:
Hostel warden's note, senior block, Tuesday

Dolma has been falling asleep in morning prep all week. When I asked, she showed me her phone: forty-two messages from Kunal between midnight and three, most of them about his parents' arguments at home and whether his marks are good enough. She said she answers every one because he is her closest friend and she does not want him to feel alone.

She also said, very quietly, "Sometimes I start to hate seeing his name." Then she looked ashamed of saying it.

We talked about how caring for a friend does not mean being on call all night. She decided to tell him she will reply until ten and after breakfast, and that she still cares. She also wanted him to have more people than just her. With her permission, I spoke to the school counsellor, who will meet Kunal tomorrow. I have asked Dolma to come back on Friday and tell me how the week went.

qa.q: How many messages did Kunal send between midnight and three?
qa.a: Kunal sent forty-two messages between midnight and three.

qa.q: What does Dolma's quiet comment about Kunal's name suggest?
qa.a: It suggests Dolma is exhausted and starting to feel resentful, and then ashamed of that feeling because she cares about him.

qa.q: What limit did Dolma decide to set, and why does it help?
qa.a: Dolma decided to reply only until ten and after breakfast, which lets her keep caring for Kunal without losing sleep and growing bitter.

qa.q: How might Kunal feel when Dolma sets the new limit?
qa.a: Kunal might feel hurt or worried at first, but meeting the counsellor could give him more support than one tired friend at night.

grounding: It shows a teen worn out by a friend who leans on her at all hours, who keeps caring while setting limits and bringing in a counsellor.

passage:
Sunday, 11:15 pm

It's happening again. Phone buzzing. Yamini, third call tonight. It's been every night since the breakup, sometimes till one. I love her, I really do. But I fell asleep in the chemistry practical on Friday and Ma'am noticed. And tonight, when her name flashed, the first thing I felt was irritation, and then guilt for feeling it.

I don't want to be the friend who starts avoiding calls and says "sorry, was asleep" every night. That feels worse than being honest.

So I picked up and said it. "Yami, I'm here for you. But I can't talk past ten-thirty on school nights, I'm falling apart. Let's walk together at lunch every day this week instead. And can you please talk to your didi, or Mrs Pinto? You need more than just me."

She was quiet. Then she said, "Okay. Sorry. I didn't notice." She said she would talk to her didi tomorrow.

I feel lighter already.

— Anjali

qa.q: When did Anjali fall asleep in class?
qa.a: Anjali fell asleep in the chemistry practical on Friday.

qa.q: What did Anjali feel when Yamini's name flashed tonight?
qa.a: Anjali felt irritation first and then guilt for feeling it, because Anjali loves Yamini but is exhausted.

qa.q: What would you say Anjali got right in the phone call?
qa.a: Anjali was honest about a limit, offered another way to be there at lunch, and pointed Yamini to her didi and Mrs Pinto.

qa.q: How might Yamini see Anjali's limit?
qa.a: Yamini may feel a bit embarrassed at not noticing, but also still cared for, since Anjali offered daily lunch walks.

grounding: It shows a teen worn out by a friend who calls every night, who cares, sets a limit and encourages other support instead of quietly resenting the friend.

passage:
Okay, so you asked what I'm proud of from Class 10? This is going to sound small. I'm Madhuri, and I kept a secret for a whole year.

My friend Neelam was the anonymous poet in the school magazine. "Moth." Everyone wanted to know who Moth was. Neelam only told me because she was terrified of people reading her poems while knowing it was her.

People guessed me. Then they guessed that I knew. The boys in our row would chant "Mo-oth" when I walked in. One girl said she'd stop being my friend unless I told her. I just shrugged, every time.

It wasn't all easy. Once I asked Neelam, "Is hiding this making you feel worse? You can tell people any time, you know." She said no, it made her feel free. So I kept going.

At the farewell, Neelam read a Moth poem on stage, by her own choice. The hall went wild. I cried more than she did.

qa.q: What name did Neelam use in the school magazine?
qa.a: Neelam used the name "Moth" in the school magazine.

qa.q: What was Neelam feeling about people knowing she wrote the poems?
qa.a: Neelam felt terrified of people reading her poems while knowing they were hers, which is why she kept it secret.

qa.q: Why was it wise for Madhuri to ask Neelam whether hiding the secret made her feel worse?
qa.a: It checked that the secret was not hurting Neelam, so Madhuri's loyalty stayed about Neelam's wellbeing and not only about silence.

qa.q: What would have changed if Madhuri had given in to the girl who threatened the friendship?
qa.a: Neelam's trust would have been broken, and she might never have chosen to read her poem on stage in her own time.

grounding: It shows a teen keeping a friend's harmless secret through teasing and pressure, with loyalty as a strength, while checking that the secret is not hurting the friend.

Monday. Dilnaz told Eshaan at the bus stop, cheeks pink, that she'd signed up for the Kathak exam in secret. "Not my family, not the class. If I fail, nobody needs to know." Eshaan promised.

Thursday. Someone had seen Dilnaz near the dance academy. In the classroom, three boys cornered Eshaan. "You're her best friend. Where does she go every Thursday? Tell, na." One grabbed his notebook and waved it. "Secret boyfriend?" Eshaan grabbed it back. "Ask her yourself." They called him boring for the rest of the day.

Saturday. Eshaan found Dilnaz outside the academy after practice. "People are asking. I'm not saying anything. But is keeping this secret making things harder for you? Like, are you okay?" Dilnaz thought, then smiled. "I'm fine. It's just mine for now. After the exam I'll tell everyone." She bought him a cutting chai from the stall to say thanks.

passage:
Volleyball coach's note, under-17 girls, end of month

Rukmini from Class 8 has attached herself to Nikita, our captain. She copies Nikita's hairband, her serve, even her water bottle. In the dressing room I heard her say, "You're my hero, didi. I tell you everything." And she does: marks, fights at home, all of it.

Nikita clearly enjoys it, and also looks tired by it. Last week she told Rukmini to stop sitting with her Class 8 friends because "they're not serious." Rukmini did it at once. I saw Nikita notice that, and look uncomfortable.

On Wednesday Nikita came to me. "I don't want her to think I'm perfect. And I shouldn't be deciding who her friends are." We agreed she would tell Rukmini about her own missed serves in last year's final and apologise about the friends comment. I said I would check in with Rukmini weekly, and Nikita suggested Rukmini talk to her elder sister as well.

Nikita did both on Thursday. Rukmini sat with her Class 8 friends at lunch again.

qa.q: What did Nikita tell Rukmini about her Class 8 friends?
qa.a: Nikita told Rukmini to stop sitting with her Class 8 friends because "they're not serious."

qa.q: What was Nikita feeling when Rukmini obeyed at once?
qa.a: Nikita felt uncomfortable and a little uneasy, realising how much power Rukmini's admiration was giving her.

qa.q: What steps did Nikita and the coach agree on, and why were they wise?
qa.a: Nikita would share her own missed serves and apologise, and the coach would check in weekly, so Rukmini sees Nikita's flaws and has other support.

qa.q: What is it like for Rukmini to hear that her hero made mistakes too?
qa.a: It may surprise Rukmini, but it could also relieve her, showing that she does not have to be perfect either.

grounding: It shows a teen who is idolised by a younger friend, feels proud and pressured, stays honest about her flaws and points the younger friend to other supports instead of controlling her.

passage:
Wed night

Vinita from the second floor told me today, "You're literally my hero, Rekha didi." She's in Class 7. She knocks every evening now and tells me everything: her friends, the boy who teased her, what her mum said at dinner. She even asked which subjects she should take in Class 9 because "whatever you say is right."

Honestly it felt amazing for about a minute. Then it felt heavy. I'm not always right. I failed my maths unit test last week and cried in the bathroom.

I noticed I could tell her anything and she'd just do it. That scared me more than anything.

So today I told her about the maths test. She stared. "You? Failed?" I said, "Yes, I mess up a lot. For subject choices, ask your mum and the school counsellor, they'll know more than me." She looked disappointed, then said, "Okay. But can I still come and talk?"

Of course she can.

— Rekha

qa.a: Vinita is in Class 7.

qa.q: What did Rekha feel after Vinita called Rekha a hero?
qa.a: Rekha felt proud for a moment, then weighed down and even scared by how easily Vinita would follow anything Rekha said.

qa.q: Which choice worked, and why?
qa.a: Telling Vinita about the failed maths test and pointing her to her mum and the counsellor worked, because it was honest and gave Vinita other people to rely on.

qa.q: How might Vinita see Rekha after hearing about the maths test?
qa.a: Vinita may be surprised and a bit disappointed at first, but still trusts Rekha enough to want to keep talking.

grounding: It shows a teen idolised by a younger friend who shares everything, feeling proud and pressured, staying honest about flaws and pointing her to other supports.

"Jomon, your turn. Jump from the wall to the shed roof." Vishal pointed. The others were already cheering.

Jomon looked at the gap. "No."

"Come on, it's not that far. Everyone did it."

"I said no."

"Why? Scared?"

Jomon felt his face heat up. The words "sorry, it's just my ankle" were right on his tongue, and they weren't even true. He swallowed them. "No is my answer. That's it."

A couple of the boys groaned. One said, "Boring."

Vishal was quiet for a second. Then he shrugged. "Okay. Fine. Your call." He turned to the others. "Leave him. Who wants to go get samosas instead?"

"You're not annoyed?" Jomon asked as they walked.

"A bit," Vishal admitted. "But I'd rather you say no than fake it and break your leg."

Jomon laughed, the awkwardness loosening. "Thanks."

"Just don't tell anyone I was the sensible one."

qa.q: What dare did Vishal give Jomon?
qa.a: Vishal dared Jomon to jump from the wall to the shed roof.

qa.q: What was Jomon feeling when he almost made up an excuse about his ankle?
qa.a: Jomon felt embarrassed and awkward, with his face heating up, and wanted to soften the no with a false reason.

qa.q: Why was it better for Jomon not to say sorry or invent a reason?
qa.a: A plain no was enough, and inventing a sorry excuse would have treated his boundary as something to apologise for.

qa.q: How does Vishal see Jomon's refusal in the end?
qa.a: Vishal is a little annoyed but respects it, saying he would rather Jomon say no than get hurt faking courage.

grounding: It shows a teen saying no to a dare, feeling awkward, not apologising or giving a reason, and a good friend accepting it.

passage:
At the Class 12 farewell last year, everyone was hugging. Ramesh, who sat behind me for two years, came towards me with his arms open. I'm Mehak, and I don't really like hugs, not even from people I like.

I stepped back and said, "Not a hug, sorry, I'm just not…" and then I heard myself. Sorry. Why was I sorry? I tried again. "No hug. High five?"

The moment felt about ten seconds long. My cheeks were burning. A girl near us laughed, not meanly, but I wanted to disappear.

Ramesh just held up his hand. "High five it is." We slapped hands and he said, "Good luck for college, Mehak." Then he went to find his other friends.

Afterwards I kept thinking about that first "sorry." I didn't owe anyone a reason. The second answer was the real one. Ramesh made it easy, and that's how I knew he was a good friend.

qa.q: What did Mehak offer instead of a hug?
qa.a: Mehak offered a high five.

qa.q: What was Mehak feeling right after stepping back?
qa.a: Mehak felt embarrassed and self-conscious, with burning cheeks, and wanted to disappear when a girl laughed.

qa.q: What did Mehak notice about the first answer, and why does that matter?
qa.a: Mehak noticed the automatic "sorry" and changed to a plain no, which matters because a boundary needs no apology or reason.

qa.q: How might Ramesh see the moment?
qa.a: Ramesh seems to take it easily and without offence, accepting the high five and wishing Mehak luck as a friend would.

grounding: It shows a teen saying no to a hug, feeling awkward, dropping the apology and a good friend accepting it without fuss.

The school fest was deafening. The DJ was ten minutes from shutting down, and Jahnavi had one plan: a selfie with Rekha, the girl she'd liked all year, to post before the night ended.

She found Rekha near the food stalls. "Quick photo? For my profile?" She was already holding up her phone.

Rekha hesitated, then leaned close to be heard over the speakers. "Can we not? I'm not comfortable with it going online. Sorry."

Jahnavi felt her stomach drop. For a second she wanted to say, "It's just one photo," or pull a sad face until Rekha gave in. She could feel the time running out.

She lowered the phone. "No, that's totally fine. Thanks for telling me straight."

Rekha smiled, surprised. "You're not upset?"

"A little disappointed. That's mine to deal with." Jahnavi nodded at the stalls. "Want to split a plate of pani puri before they close?"

They did, shouting over the music.

qa.a: Jahnavi found Rekha near the food stalls.

qa.q: What did Jahnavi feel when Rekha said no to the photo?
qa.a: Jahnavi felt disappointed, with her stomach dropping, and was briefly tempted to push or sulk to change Rekha's mind.

qa.q: Which choice worked, and why?
qa.a: Lowering the phone at once and thanking Rekha for being straight worked, because it respected the boundary and kept the evening friendly.

qa.q: What is it like for Rekha when Jahnavi does not sulk?
qa.a: Rekha seems surprised and relieved, and probably feels safer being honest with Jahnavi in future.

grounding: It shows a teen whose crush says she is not comfortable with something, who stops at once, thanks her for honesty and does not pout.

Tejas had been calling Ira every night that week, sometimes past eleven. He liked her so much it made him stupid, Darshan said.

On Friday, on the walk back from the metro, Ira said, "Tejas, can I say something? The late calls. I'm not comfortable with them. My parents are strict, and I need to sleep."

Tejas's chest tightened. He'd thought she liked the calls. Part of him wanted to say, "But you always pick up," or go quiet for days.

"Okay," he said. "No more late calls. Thanks for saying it, really."

"You're sure you're not upset?"

"I'm a bit embarrassed. But I'd rather know."

That evening Darshan poked him on the colony stairs. "Bro, she dumped you or what? Sulk a bit, make her feel bad, she'll call you herself."

Tejas shook his head. "No. She told me what she's okay with. I'm not playing games."

At eight the next evening, Ira texted him a photo of her cat. He grinned for an hour.

You want to know why I started the peer support group? It's because of Class 9. I'm Baljeet, and there was this older girl in the tuition centre, Rukmini, from Class 12. She was really nice to me at first. She said I was mature for my age, smarter than the boys in my class. I felt special.

Then she started asking for things. Come to her friend's flat after tuition. Don't tell my parents, they wouldn't understand. Try a drink, just one. I kept saying "maybe" because I didn't want her to stop liking me.

One evening she messaged, "Come alone tonight, and delete this chat." Something in my stomach just went cold.

I wrote back "No." That was all. I didn't explain. Then I blocked her and walked straight to the kitchen and showed my mother the whole chat.

She didn't shout. She hugged me, said it wasn't my fault, and called the tuition centre head that same night. Nobody who cares about you asks you to hide them.

qa.a: Rukmini's message asked Baljeet to come alone that night and delete the chat.

qa.q: What was Baljeet feeling when the last message arrived?
qa.a: Baljeet felt a cold fear in the stomach, sensing something was wrong after weeks of feeling special and unsure.

qa.q: Which steps did Baljeet take that were wise?
qa.a: Baljeet said a plain no, blocked Rukmini, and showed the whole chat to a parent the same evening.

qa.q: How did Baljeet's mother respond, and why did it matter?
qa.a: She stayed calm, hugged Baljeet, said it was not Baljeet's fault and called the tuition centre head that night, which made Baljeet safe and not blamed.

grounding: It shows a teen flattered and pressured by an older teen, who says no, leaves, tells a trusted adult, and learns it was not their fault.

Day one. At the tuition centre, Ramesh from the Class 12 batch told Aditi her essay was the best he had read. He started messaging her every night. "You're not like other girls in Class 9." She smiled at her phone for an hour.

Day four. His messages changed. He asked her to meet him at the empty terrace after class, "just us, don't tell anyone, your parents won't get it." Then he asked for a photo of her in her room. Aditi felt her hands go cold. She didn't send anything. She typed "maybe later" and then hated that she had.

Day six. Aditi wrote, "No. I'm not meeting you and I'm not sending anything." She blocked him. That evening she sat next to her aunt on the sofa and handed over her phone. "Masi, I think something's not right."

Masi read every message. "You did everything right. This is not your fault." She took screenshots and called the centre's director before dinner.

qa.a: Saying no, blocking Ramesh and showing Masi the messages were wise, because they ended the contact and brought in a trusted adult the same day.

The practice board result came out on Wednesday: 58 per cent. Salma folded the sheet into four and slid it under her geometry box.

At home in their Bhopal flat, Ammi was on the phone with an aunt. "Coaching fees, extra tuition, everything. We've put what we saved into this year. She'll do us proud." Salma heard it from the corridor and felt her throat close.

For two days she said the results weren't out. Her friend Damini found her crying in the library on Friday. "You can't keep hiding it. When the real result comes, it'll be ten times worse."

That evening Salma sat down with both her parents. She put the sheet on the table. "58. I'm sorry I hid it. I'm scared all the time because I know how much you've put into this. I'll work, I promise. But I can't carry everything you're hoping for. I need you to know that."

Abbu looked at the sheet a long time. Then he pushed his tea towards her. "Talk. Tell us what's heavy."

qa.a: Salma got 58 per cent.

qa.q: What was Salma feeling when she heard Ammi on the phone?
qa.a: Salma felt dread and pressure, her throat closing, because her parents had put what they saved into this year and expected her to make them proud.

qa.q: What went wrong at first, and what fixed it?
qa.a: Hiding the result for two days made Salma more anxious; telling both parents plainly and saying how much she could carry fixed it.

qa.q: How might Abbu feel when Salma says she can't carry everything?
qa.a: Abbu may feel worried and a little guilty, but he chooses to listen, pushing his tea towards her and asking what is heavy.

passage:
Friday night

Mummy checked my unit test marks at the gate today before even saying hi. 72 in physics. Her face did the thing. "Only 72, Tarun? Sharma aunty's daughter got 90." Then silence all the way home.

When I get 90, she hugs me. When I get 72, she goes cold. Sometimes I think she only loves the marks.

I stayed in my room all evening and didn't come out for dinner. Then I heard her on the phone with Nani, and she said, "I just don't want him to struggle like I did. I never got to finish college." Her voice was shaking.

I didn't know that.

I went and sat next to her. I said, "Mummy, when you go quiet after marks, it feels like you stop loving me. What would help is if we made a study plan together on Sundays, and on other nights we just have dinner without talking about tests."

She hugged me for a long time. She said yes to the Sunday plan.

qa.q: What mark did Tarun get in physics?
qa.a: Tarun got 72 in physics.

qa.q: What did Tarun feel when Mummy went quiet after seeing the marks?
qa.a: Tarun felt hurt and unloved, as if her love depended on his marks.

qa.q: What did Tarun ask for that could help both of them?
qa.a: Tarun asked for a Sunday study plan together and calm dinners on other nights without talk of tests.

qa.q: How might Mummy's own past shape the way she pushes Tarun?
qa.a: Having never finished college herself, she seems afraid he will struggle as she did, so her fear comes out as pressure.

grounding: It shows a teen who feels measured by marks and that love is conditional, who hears the fear behind the parent's push and says what helps instead of shutting down.

passage:
Dear Zoha Khala,

You asked why I sounded so low on the phone. It's Arnab. He topped the physics test again. He's topped every test this year. Every time the marks go up on the board, I feel about two inches tall.

I'm ashamed of what I did last week. He asked to borrow my lab notes because he was absent, and I said I'd lost them. I hadn't. I just didn't want to help him win again. And when someone said he must be getting papers from his tuition teacher, I nodded. I don't even believe that.

Afterwards I felt sick. So on Monday I gave him the notes and asked, honestly, how he studies. He showed me: he does old papers with a timer every Sunday, and writes down every mistake in a separate book.

I've started doing the same. I'm also trying to remember that a rank is one small number, not all of me.

Love,
Mehak

qa.q: What did Mehak say about the lab notes when Arnab asked?
qa.a: Mehak said the lab notes were lost.

qa.q: What was Mehak feeling each time the marks went up on the board?
qa.a: Mehak felt small and bitter, about two inches tall, because Arnab kept topping every test.

qa.q: What turned things around for Mehak, and why did it help?
qa.a: Giving Arnab the notes and asking how he studies turned things around, because it replaced envy and rumour with learning his timed-paper method.

qa.q: How might Arnab have felt if he heard the rumour about the tuition teacher?
qa.a: Arnab would probably feel hurt and unfairly accused, since his results came from real work like timed papers every Sunday.

grounding: It shows a teen who feels small and bitter as a classmate tops every test, stops hiding notes and nodding at rumours, and studies the classmate's method instead.

passage:
You asked why Hemant and I study together now? Fine, I'll tell you. I'm Kalyani, and for all of Class 10, I couldn't stand him. He topped maths every single time. Ninety-eight, ninety-six, a hundred. I'd sit there with my seventy-something and feel like the smallest person in the room.

The bitter part got worse. In March someone said Hemant's father knows the paper setter, and I didn't just nod. I repeated it. To three people. It wasn't true. I knew it wasn't.

Then one day I saw his rough book. Pages and pages of the same kind of problem, solved again and again. He'd stayed after school to do extra sums with Sir. That's it. That's the secret.

I felt terrible. I told those three people I'd been wrong. And then I asked Hemant if I could join his Saturday practice.

My marks went up. Not to his. But I stopped thinking a rank is the only thing that counts.

qa.q: What did Kalyani see in Hemant's rough book?
qa.a: Kalyani saw pages and pages of the same kind of problem, solved again and again.

qa.q: What did Kalyani feel after seeing Hemant's rough book?
qa.a: Kalyani felt terrible and ashamed for spreading a false rumour when Hemant's results came from hard work.

qa.q: What did Kalyani do to repair the damage?
qa.a: Kalyani told the three people the rumour was wrong and asked to join Hemant's Saturday practice.

qa.q: What is it like for Hemant when people say his father knows the paper setter?
qa.a: It would feel unfair and hurtful, as if all his extra practice counted for nothing.

grounding: It shows a teen who feels small and bitter as a classmate tops every test, spreads a rumour, then corrects it and studies the classmate's method instead.
